approach.title: One pass remembering the latest index of each word
approach.explanation: Walk the list once. Keep the most recent index where word1 appeared and the most recent index where word2 appeared. Whenever you see one of them and the other has already been seen, the gap to the other's latest index is a candidate. The closest partner for any occurrence is always the most recent occurrence of the other word to its left (or a later one, which will be handled when that later one is reached).
chooseWhen: You need only the minimum distance for one pair of words.
The list is scanned once and no index lists are needed.
tradeoffs: Building index lists for both words and merging them is equally linear but uses extra memory.
If many pairs are queried against the same list, precomputing per-word index lists pays off instead.
invariants: i1 and i2 hold the latest positions of word1 and word2 among the indices already scanned (or -1).
ans is the smallest gap between any already scanned pair.
hints: Which occurrence of word2 can be closest to a given occurrence of word1?
The best partner on the left side is the most recent one.
Track the last index of each word and update the answer whenever either word appears.

stages.explanation: Only the nearest occurrence on each side matters. Scanning left to right, the nearest one on the left is the latest one seen so far; the nearest on the right is found when that occurrence is reached.
stages.rationale: This reduces a pairwise comparison to constant work per index.
instructions: List all pairs for the first example and see which one wins.

observations: Pairs separated by another occurrence of either word are never better.
hints: Think about the most recent occurrence.

stages.rationale: Each index is processed once with constant work.
instructions: Initialise i1 = i2 = -1 and ans = len(words).
Update ans only when both indices are set.

hints: The answer is always at most n - 1, so len(words) is a safe start.

approach.title: Two pointers with a rotation map
approach.explanation: Use a map from each rotatable digit to its rotated digit. Move one pointer from the left and one from the right; the left digit's rotation must equal the right digit. The loop includes the case where the pointers meet, so the middle digit is checked against itself.
chooseWhen: You only need a yes/no answer for one string.
The symmetry is between mirrored positions.
tradeoffs: Building the rotated string and comparing is simpler but allocates a copy.
The pointer version stops at the first mismatch.
invariants: All pairs outside the current pointer window are valid rotations of each other.
hints: Which digits still look like digits upside down?
Rotation also reverses the order.
Compare the rotation of num[l] with num[r] while l <= r.

stages.title: Model the rotation
stages.question: What does rotating the whole string do?
stages.explanation: Each digit is replaced by its rotated digit and the order is reversed. So the string is unchanged exactly when rotate(num[i]) == num[n-1-i] for all i.
stages.rationale: This turns a geometric statement into a pairwise check.
observations: 6 and 9 swap, which is why 69 works.
hints: Do not forget the reversal.

stages.title: Implement the pointer check
stages.question: How do you test all pairs in one loop?
stages.explanation: Start l = 0 and r = n - 1; while l <= r, fail if num[l] is not in the map or its image differs from num[r]; then move both pointers.
stages.rationale: The condition l <= r covers the middle digit.
observations: Using l < r would skip the middle check.
hints: Check membership before looking up the image.

approach.title: Build from the middle outwards
approach.explanation: A strobogrammatic number of length n is a valid pair (0-0, 1-1, 6-9, 8-8, 9-6) wrapped around a strobogrammatic core of length n - 2. Start from the empty core (even n) or the three self-rotating digits (odd n) and wrap pairs until the length is n, skipping the 0-0 pair on the outermost layer.
chooseWhen: You must enumerate all answers, not count them.
The structure is naturally recursive: outer pair plus inner core.
tradeoffs: Generating all n-digit numbers and testing them is exponential in n with base 10 instead of 5.
Recursion depth is n/2, which is tiny here.
invariants: Every string at a recursion level of length L is strobogrammatic of length L (allowing inner zeros).

Remove them; what is left?
Recurse on n - 2 and wrap each pair, skipping 0-0 at the outermost level.

approach.explanation: Adding one changes the rightmost digit that is not 9 by +1 and turns all digits after it into 0. If every digit is 9, the result is 1 followed by zeros. approach.title: Difference array with a final prefix sum

A Fenwick or segment tree is needed only if reads are interleaved with updates.
